standard.title: Causes and Effects of the Industrial Revolution
standard.description: the social, economic, political, technological and/or environmental causes and effects of the Industrial Revolution on Europe in the late 18th and 19th century
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied pre-modern societies in Year 8 including Medieval Europe and early empires. They understand concepts of economic and social change, power, and significant events. This descriptor introduces the Industrial Revolution as the defining transformation of the modern period — students have general awareness but have not analytically examined its causes or its multi-dimensional effects.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the social, economic, political, technological and/or environmental causes and effects of the Industrial Revolution on Europe in the late 18th and 19th century.

nodes.label: Technological changes and the factory system
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how key technological changes — steam power, railways, factories — drove the development of industrialised cities and transformed the economy.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how one technological change (e.g. steam power or the railway) contributed to industrialisation.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how changes in technology — steam-driven spinning mills, railways, steam ships, and the development of iron and steel production — led to the factory system and the growth of industrial cities; identify the spread of these innovations across Europe, the USA and Japan.
wider: Investigate the development of the railway network as a transformative technology — examining how it physically reshaped cities, enabled industrial distribution, and created new patterns of work and travel
Examine the spread of industrialisation beyond Britain to continental Europe, the USA and Japan — comparing the pace and triggers of industrialisation in different national contexts
Investigate how steam-powered textile mills transformed the textile industry — examining the human consequences of mechanisation for hand-weavers and cottage industry workers
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the technological drivers of industrialisation is the foundation for understanding all subsequent social, economic, political, and environmental effects. Without a clear picture of what the Industrial Revolution involved technologically, students cannot explain why society changed so rapidly or why conditions in factories and cities were so extreme.

response_modes.reason: Students need to understand the causal mechanism — how technology created factories, which required urban labour, which drove urbanisation — before examining effects on specific groups. Model the chain explicitly.

success_criteria: Explains at least two technological changes and connects each to the development of the factory system or industrialised cities
Identifies how at least one innovation spread beyond Britain

nodes.label: Multiple causes of the Industrial Revolution
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse multiple factors that caused the Industrial Revolution, explaining how they interacted to make industrialisation possible.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and describe at least three factors that caused the Industrial Revolution.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the multiple causes of the Industrial Revolution including: the Agricultural Revolution (freeing labour), Enlightenment ideas (valuing reason and progress), access to raw materials (coal, iron), growing population, a wealthy middle class, increased individual freedom, access to cheap labour, transport improvements, inventions and innovation, trade and commerce, and an expanding empire providing markets and raw materials.
wider: Examine the role of Britain's colonial empire in enabling the Industrial Revolution — providing raw materials (cotton from India, USA; minerals from colonies) and markets for manufactured goods — assessing how industrialisation and imperialism were mutually reinforcing

Investigate the role of Enlightenment thinking in creating a cultural environment favourable to invention and commerce — examining how ideas about progress, rationality, and individual liberty shaped attitudes toward innovation

Examine the Agricultural Revolution as a precondition for the Industrial Revolution — tracing how enclosures, new farming techniques, and mechanisation freed labour and created the urban workforce that factories required

response_modes.reason: The multi-causal nature of the Industrial Revolution is important to establish — single-cause explanations (e.g. 'steam power caused it') are inadequate. Widening across economic, social, and colonial causes gives a more complete and historically accurate picture.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The multi-causal analysis of the Industrial Revolution is a pedagogically rich opportunity for developing genuinely complex historical thinking — examining how structural, ideological, and material conditions combined to produce a transformative event. The connection between industrialisation and imperialism is particularly important for understanding global history.
success_criteria: Identifies and describes at least four causes of the Industrial Revolution from different categories (technological, economic, social, colonial)
Explains how at least two causes interacted — demonstrating causal complexity rather than parallel listing

nodes.label: Most significant effects of the Industrial Revolution
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the most significant effects of the Industrial Revolution, including economic growth, social restructuring, changing working conditions, and environmental impacts.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least three effects of the Industrial Revolution across different domains (social, economic, environmental, or political).
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate the most significant effects of the Industrial Revolution including: economic growth and capital accumulation; changing economic and social structures (rise of the middle class, new working class); changes in working conditions (factory labour, urbanisation); rising standards of living (for some); new ideas (capitalism, socialism, nationalism); imperialism; and environmental impacts (pollution, resource extraction, urban crowding).
wider: Evaluate the environmental impact of the Industrial Revolution — examining river pollution, air quality in industrial cities, and coal extraction — and assess how early industrial environmentalism (e.g. public health reform) responded to these conditions

Examine the rise of the industrial middle class as a new social force — analysing how factory owners, managers, and professionals displaced the aristocracy's economic dominance while maintaining social conservatism

Investigate how the Industrial Revolution created the material conditions for both capitalism (private ownership of factories) and the socialist critique of capitalism (Marx, Engels writing in Manchester) — examining how the same conditions produced opposing ideological responses

response_modes.reason: Evaluation of the most significant effects integrates all preceding knowledge of the Industrial Revolution — requiring students to weigh causes and effects across multiple domains rather than describing each independently.

success_criteria: Describes at least four effects of the Industrial Revolution across at least two different domains
Evaluates at least one effect as most significant with supporting historical reasoning
